name: Stone-Campbell Movement
summary: The American movement to restore New Testament Christianity without creeds, led by Barton W. Stone and Thomas and Alexander Campbell, which produced the Churches of Christ, the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), and the independent Christian Churches.
place: Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Virginia (now West Virginia), and the American frontier

start.label: Barton Stone's group dissolves the Springfield Presbytery to be 'Christians only'

end.label: Stone's Christians and Campbell's Disciples unite at Lexington, Kentucky

key_dates.label: The Campbells' Brush Run church joins the Redstone Baptist Association
Alexander Campbell begins The Christian Baptist
Campbell's 'Reformers' separate from the Baptists; the Millennial Harbinger begins

background.text: Barton W. Stone, a Presbyterian minister, hosted the Cane Ridge revival (1801); he and others who preached free salvation for all were censured by the Synod of Kentucky and formed their own Springfield Presbytery (1803).

Thomas Campbell, a Seceder Presbyterian minister from Ireland, was censured in Pennsylvania (1807) for giving communion to Presbyterians of other branches; he and his son Alexander called for Christian unity on the Bible alone.

happened.text: In The Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery (1804), Stone's group dissolved their presbytery 'to sink into union with the Body of Christ at large' and called themselves simply Christians.

Thomas Campbell's Declaration and Address (1809) argued that 'the church of Christ upon earth is essentially, intentionally, and constitutionally one' and that nothing should be required of Christians that the Bible does not expressly teach.
The Campbells adopted believers' baptism by immersion (1812), taught weekly communion and the independence of congregations, and Alexander Campbell became a leading debater and editor.
Stone's and Campbell's followers united in 1832, sealed by a handshake between 'Raccoon' John Smith and Stone at Lexington, Kentucky.

participants.name: Barton W. Stone
participants.role: Founder of the 'Christian' churches in Kentucky

participants.name: Thomas Campbell
participants.role: Author of the Declaration and Address

participants.name: Alexander Campbell
participants.role: Leading preacher, editor, and founder of Bethany College (1840)

participants.name: Walter Scott
participants.role: Evangelist who taught a 'five-finger' plan of salvation

participants.name: 'Raccoon' John Smith
participants.role: Preacher who helped unite the two groups

outcomes.text: Disputes over instrumental music in worship and missionary societies divided the movement; the U.S. religious census of 1906 listed the a cappella Churches of Christ separately from the Disciples of Christ.
A second division followed in the 20th century, when congregations opposed to the Disciples' liberal theology and 1968 restructuring formed the independent Christian Churches and Churches of Christ.
The three branches together have millions of members, mostly in the United States.

condemnations_note: The movement's founders were censured by the churches they came from, though not excommunicated in the strict sense.

condemnations.reason: Richard McNemar and John Thompson censured for preaching against Calvinist doctrine; Stone and three others withdrew with them and were suspended
Thomas Campbell censured for giving communion to Presbyterians outside his branch
condemnations.status: Campbell withdrew from the synod in 1808

condemnations.by: Baptist associations, including the Dover Association of Virginia (1830)
condemnations.reason: Churches and preachers following Alexander Campbell ('Reformers') excluded

persecution_note: No members of the movement were arrested or executed for their faith; opposition took the form of church censures and exclusion.
